name: Kilwa Sultanate
summary: A Swahili trading state on an island off Tanzania whose authority at its height stretched along the whole Swahili Coast. It grew rich on gold from Great Zimbabwe and Indian Ocean trade.

location.value: Kilwa Kisiwani, an island off southern Tanzania, with authority at its height over the whole Swahili Coast.

terrain.value: Coral islands, mangrove creeks and a monsoon-swept coast facing the Indian Ocean.
terrain.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

climate.value: Tropical, with monsoon winds that set the rhythm of sea trade.
climate.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

resources.value: Control of the gold trade from Sofala (from the Great Zimbabwe region), ivory and timber.
resources.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

disasters.value: No major natural disasters are recorded.
disasters.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

population.value: No reliable estimate; Kilwa town may have had around 10,000 people at its height.
population.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

urbanisation.value: Stone towns with coral-stone mosques and palaces, such as Husuni Kubwa.
urbanisation.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

disease.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

migration.value: Legend says it was founded by Ali ibn al-Hassan Shirazi, a prince from Shiraz in Persia; historians debate how far this reflects real migration.

economicBase.value: Sofala was the main entrepot for the gold and ivory trade and its acquisition brought the Kilwa sultans a windfall of gold revenue. The slave trade is not mentioned.

tradeRoutes.value: Indian Ocean routes to Arabia, Persia, India and China; gold from Sofala.
tradeRoutes.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; Kilwa minted its own copper coins and Chinese porcelain has been found there.
wealth.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

moneyAndTax.value: Copper (and some silver) coins minted from about the 11th century; customs duties on gold.
moneyAndTax.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

inequality.value: A Muslim merchant aristocracy above townspeople and slaves.
inequality.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

governmentType.value: A sultanate: the Shirazi dynasty to about 1277, then the Mahdali dynasty of Yemeni Arab sayyids to about 1495.

keyRulers.value: Ali ibn al-Hassan Shirazi, a Persian prince, is the legendary founder (10th century; the infobox gives 957). Al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman ruled from 1310 for 24 years and died without heirs; the page does not describe a peak under him.

succession.value: Hereditary, with disputes between rival branches.
succession.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

institutions.value: Islamic law and a merchant elite around the sultan.
institutions.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

stability.value: Prosperous in the 13th–14th centuries; weakened by disputes in the 15th.
stability.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

eliteConflict.value: Rival claimants and competition with Mombasa.
eliteConflict.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

armyAndTech.value: Small forces; defended by its island position.
armyAndTech.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

majorWars.value: In 1505 Francisco de Almeida landed about 500 Portuguese soldiers, drove out Emir Ibrahim and installed Muhammad Arcone as a vassal sultan. The infobox gives 1513 as the end.

territoryChange.value: At its height its authority stretched over the entire length of the Swahili Coast.

alliancesRivals.value: Rival of Mombasa and other Swahili towns; attacked by Portugal.
alliancesRivals.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

inventions.value: Coral-stone architecture with domes and vaults.
inventions.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

scienceEducation.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

openness.value: A cosmopolitan port where Africans, Arabs and Persians met.
openness.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

communicationTransport.value: Dhows sailing with the monsoon winds to Arabia and India; coastal boats to Sofala.

religion.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

languageWriting.value: Swahili, a Bantu language with many Arabic words; Arabic for religion.
languageWriting.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

artsArchitecture.value: The Great Mosque of Kilwa and the palace of Husuni Kubwa (UNESCO World Heritage Site).
artsArchitecture.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

socialStructure.value: Sultan, merchant families, townspeople and slaves.
socialStructure.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

sharedIdentity.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

dailyLife.value: Coral-stone houses for merchants; mud and thatch for others; rice, fish and coconut.

neighbours.value: Mombasa, Zanzibar, Sofala and inland kingdoms.
neighbours.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

ideasReligions.value: Helped spread Islam along the East African coast.
ideasReligions.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

colonisation.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

riseSignals.value: Taking control of the Sofala gold trade in the 12th–13th centuries.
riseSignals.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

peakPeriod.value: The page places the sultanate’s zenith in the 15th century, after it acquired Sofala; this conflicts with the entry’s earlier 13th–14th-century peak.

declineSignals.value: Falling gold trade and the Portuguese attack.
declineSignals.source: Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)

outcome.value: Never regained its power after the Portuguese sack; dates for its end vary.

sources.value: The Kilwa Chronicle, archaeology, Ibn Battuta’s visit (1331). Checked against Wikipedia (“Kilwa Sultanate”).

overallCertainty.value: Medium. Its founding legend and early dates are debated.

knownFor.label: Husuni Kubwa palace
knownFor.note: A huge coral-stone palace with a pool, overlooking the sea.

knownFor.label: Great Mosque of Kilwa
knownFor.note: A domed mosque admired by Ibn Battuta.

knownFor.label: Kilwa copper coins
knownFor.note: Some of the earliest coins minted in sub-Saharan Africa.
